# Headline result

Let

\[
(p_i,z_{i,0}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
\]

be independent copies of \((P,Z_0)\), where \(P\in\{-1,1\}\). The label \(p_i\) remains fixed; only \(z_{i,k}\) is trained.

Define

\[
\phi(z)=\arctan z,
\qquad
f_{n,k}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\phi(z_{i,k}),
\qquad
r_{n,k}=f_{n,k}-y.
\]

Exact finite-width GD is

\[
z_{i,k+1}
=
z_{i,k}
-
\eta_n p_i r_{n,k}\phi'(z_{i,k}).
\]

Use the physical clock

\[
t=k\eta_n.
\]

Assume

\[
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n\longrightarrow0.
\]

Equivalently, it is enough to assume

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n\longrightarrow0.
\]

The limiting population state is

\[
\mu_t=\operatorname{Law}(P,X(t)),
\]

where

\[
F(z)=z+\frac{z^3}{3},
\qquad
X(0)=F(Z_0),
\qquad
Z(t)=F^{-1}(X(t)).
\]

Its residual and dynamics are

\[
r(t)=\mathbb E[P\phi(Z(t))]-y,
\]

\[
\frac{dX(t)}{dt}=-P\,r(t).
\]

This is autonomous: the current law \(\mu_t\) determines \(r(t)\), and \(r(t)\) determines the next movement.

For every fixed \(T\) and every fixed bounded function \(\psi(p,z)\) that is Lipschitz in \(z\),

\[
\boxed{
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi(p_i,z_i^{\mathrm{GD}}(t))
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z(t))]
\right|
\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{in probability}.
}
\]

Choosing

\[
\psi(p,z)=p\phi(z)
\]

gives convergence of the prediction, residual, and normalized loss.

---

## 1. Raw finite GD versus transformed finite flow

Let

\[
q(z)=\phi'(z)=\frac1{1+z^2},
\qquad
X=F(z)=z+\frac{z^3}{3}.
\]

Because

\[
F'(z)=\frac1{q(z)},
\]

the raw continuous gradient flow

\[
\dot z_i=-p_i r_nq(z_i)
\]

becomes exactly

\[
\dot X_i=-p_i r_n.
\]

The coordinate transformation is exact in continuous time, but not for discrete GD.

Let

\[
v_i=-p_i r_n.
\]

One GD step is

\[
z_i^+=z_i+\eta_nq(z_i)v_i.
\]

Since \(F\) is cubic,

\[
\begin{aligned}
F(z_i^+)
={}&F(z_i)+\eta_n v_i
\\
&+\eta_n^2z_iq(z_i)^2v_i^2
+\frac{\eta_n^3}{3}q(z_i)^3v_i^3.
\end{aligned}
\]

In the toy system, \(|v_i|\) is uniformly bounded, so the accumulated GD-to-flow error is \(O(\eta_n)\).

The full neural-network proof has a backpropagated field whose normalized norm is bounded, but whose largest coordinate may be \(\sqrt n\) times larger. Its one-step coordinate defect is therefore bounded by

\[
C_T\left(\eta_n^2\sqrt n+\eta_n^3n\right).
\]

There is also an ordinary ODE local defect \(O_T(\eta_n^2)\). Over approximately \(T/\eta_n\) steps, stability gives

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
d_n\!\left(
\theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t),
\theta_n^{\mathrm{flow}}(t)
\right)
\le
C_T\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\right).
\]

Thus the first approximation vanishes under

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n\to0.
\]

For the toy model this condition is stronger than necessary, but it makes the consolidated statement compatible with the full proof.

---

## 2. Finite flow versus coarse finite Euler

Choose an auxiliary proof mesh \(\delta>0\), independent of \(\eta_n\).

Finite transformed Euler is

\[
X^n_{i,m+1}
=
X^n_{i,m}-\delta p_i r^n_m,
\]

where

\[
r^n_m
=
\frac1n\sum_j
p_j\phi\!\left(F^{-1}(X^n_{j,m})\right)-y.
\]

The transformed vector field is bounded and Lipschitz. Ordinary Euler analysis therefore gives

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
\max_i
|X_i^{n,\mathrm{flow}}(t)-X_i^{n,\mathrm{Euler}}(t)|
\le
C_T\delta,
\]

uniformly in \(n\).

Thus

\[
\text{raw GD}
\approx
\text{finite Euler}
\]

with error at most

\[
C_T\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n+\delta
\right).
\]

The coarse scheme has only

\[
M=\left\lceil\frac T\delta\right\rceil
\]

updates, which is fixed while \(n\to\infty\).

---

## 3. Pop Euler and the finite oracle

Pop Euler is

\[
r_m
=
\mathbb E\!\left[
P\phi(F^{-1}(X_m))
\right]-y,
\]

\[
X_{m+1}=X_m-\delta P r_m.
\]

The finite oracle starts from the same finite initialization as finite Euler but uses the pop residual:

\[
\bar X_{i,m+1}
=
\bar X_{i,m}-\delta p_i r_m.
\]

Its empirical residual is

\[
\bar r^n_m
=
\frac1n\sum_i
p_i\phi(F^{-1}(\bar X_{i,m}))-y,
\]

but the oracle does not use this number in its updates.

Let

\[
E_m=\max_i|X^n_{i,m}-\bar X_{i,m}|.
\]

Subtracting the finite-Euler and oracle updates gives

\[
E_{m+1}
\le
E_m+\delta|r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Insert \(\bar r^n_m\):

\[
|r^n_m-r_m|
\le
|r^n_m-\bar r^n_m|
+
|\bar r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Because \(\phi\circ F^{-1}\) is 1-Lipschitz,

\[
|r^n_m-\bar r^n_m|\le E_m.
\]

Therefore

\[
E_{m+1}
\le
(1+\delta)E_m
+
\delta|\bar r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Since \(E_0=0\),

\[
\max_{m\le M}E_m
\le
(e^T-1)
\max_{m\le M}|\bar r^n_m-r_m|.
\]

Thus finite Euler is close to the oracle whenever the oracle’s residual sampling error is small.

---

## 4. Oracle sampling versus pop Euler

The pop residual sequence

\[
r_0,\ldots,r_{M-1}
\]

is deterministic once the initial population law is fixed.

Each complete oracle trajectory is therefore a deterministic function of its own initialization:

\[
(p_i,\bar X_{i,0})
\longmapsto
(p_i,\bar X_{i,0},\ldots,\bar X_{i,M}).
\]

Hence the complete oracle trajectories are independent copies of the pop Euler trajectory.

At every step \(m\),

\[
p_i\phi(F^{-1}(\bar X_{i,m}))
\]

are independent copies of

\[
P\phi(F^{-1}(X_m)).
\]

Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound give, with probability at least \(1-\alpha/2\),

\[
\max_{m\le M}|\bar r^n_m-r_m|
\le
\pi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\max_{m\le M}E_m
\le
(e^T-1)\pi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
}.
\]

There is also a separate sampling error for the chosen observable \(\psi\). Let

\[
B_\psi=\sup\psi-\inf\psi.
\]

With probability at least \(1-\alpha/2\),

\[
\max_{m\le M}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_i\psi(p_i,\bar Z_{i,m})
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z_m)]
\right|
\le
B_\psi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
},
\]

where

\[
\bar Z_{i,m}=F^{-1}(\bar X_{i,m}),
\qquad
Z_m=F^{-1}(X_m).
\]

The first sampling term controls residual feedback. The second controls the empirical \(\psi\)-avg directly.

For complete trajectories, define

\[
\Gamma_i
=
(p_i,\bar Z_{i,0},\ldots,\bar Z_{i,M}),
\]

and

\[
\Gamma=(P,Z_0,\ldots,Z_M).
\]

The \(\Gamma_i\) are independent copies of \(\Gamma\). Therefore, for every integrable trajectory observable \(\Psi\),

\[
\frac1n\sum_i\Psi(\Gamma_i)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E[\Psi(\Gamma)].
\]

Independence is across complete particle trajectories, not across time within one trajectory.

---

## 5. Pop Euler versus pop flow

The pop flow is

\[
\dot X(t)=-P r(t),
\qquad
r(t)=\mathbb E[P\phi(F^{-1}(X(t)))]-y.
\]

Write

\[
X(t)=X_0-Ps(t).
\]

\[
\frac{ds(t)}{dt}
=
\mathbb E\!\left[
P\phi(F^{-1}(X_0-Ps(t)))
\right]-y.
\]

\[
\max_{m\delta\le T}|s_m-s(m\delta)|
\le
\frac R2(e^T-1)\delta,
\qquad
R=\frac\pi2+|y|.
\]

\[
X_m=X_0-Ps_m,
\qquad
X(t)=X_0-Ps(t),
\]

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
|X^{\mathrm{pop\ Euler}}(t)-X^{\mathrm{pop\ flow}}(t)|
\le
C_T\delta.
\]

## 6. Add the five errors

For any time \(t\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
&
\left|
\frac1n\sum_i\psi(p_i,z_i^{\mathrm{GD}}(t))
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z(t))]
\right|
\\
&\le
|\text{finite GD avg}-\text{finite flow avg}|
&&\text{(actual step)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{finite flow avg}-\text{finite Euler avg}|
&&\text{(finite mesh)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{finite Euler avg}-\text{oracle avg}|
&&\text{(feedback)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{oracle avg}-\text{pop Euler avg}|
&&\text{(sampling of }\psi\text{)}
\\
&\quad+
|\text{pop Euler avg}-\text{pop flow avg}|
&&\text{(pop mesh)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(\psi\) is \(L_\psi\)-Lipschitz in \(z\), the five terms are bounded by

\[
L_\psi C_T
\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\right),
\]

\[
L_\psi C_T\delta,
\]

\[
L_\psi(e^T-1)\pi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
},
\]

\[
B_\psi
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
},
\]

and

\[
L_\psi C_T\delta.
\]

Therefore, with probability at least \(1-\alpha\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
&
\sup_{t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_i\psi(p_i,z_i^{\mathrm{GD}}(t))
-
\mathbb E[\psi(P,Z(t))]
\right|
\\
&\le
L_\psi C_T
\left(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\right)
\\
&\quad+
2L_\psi C_T\delta
\\
&\quad+
\left[
L_\psi(e^T-1)\pi+B_\psi
\right]
\sqrt{
\frac{\log(4(M+1)/\alpha)}{2n}
}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now:

1. Choose \(\delta\) small enough to control both mesh errors.
2. Keep \(\delta\) fixed and take \(n\to\infty\).
3. The learning-rate term vanishes because

   \[
   \eta_n\sqrt n\to0.
   \]

4. The two sampling terms vanish because \(M\) is fixed.
5. Finally let \(\delta\to0\).

This proves uniform compact-time convergence in probability.

The theorem in the audited document fixes

\[
\eta_n=n^{-2},
\]

which satisfies

\[
\eta_n\sqrt n=n^{-3/2}\to0.
\]

More generally, the displayed proof estimate closes for every learning-rate sequence satisfying

\[
\eta_n=o(n^{-1/2}).
\]

I’m rebuilding it as one continuous story, defining each mathematical requirement exactly when it becomes necessary and translating terms like “well posed,” “Markovian,” and “joint limit” into concrete training statements.

Think of the theorem as trying to validate a new training simulator. The original simulator is a random width-\(n\) network updated in discrete steps of size \(\eta\). The proposed replacement is a deterministic population-level system evolving continuously in time. The theorem must show both that the replacement can run by itself and that it actually reproduces the original simulator as \(n\to\infty\) and \(\eta\to0\).

The limiting system has only three named evolving objects,

\[
z^{(1)},\qquad W^{(2)},\qquad \overline W^{(3)},
\]

but it is not finite-dimensional in the strict sense. This is like a PDE with only three fields: finitely many equations, but each field contains infinitely many degrees of freedom. Here \(z^{(1)}\) describes a whole first-layer population, \(\overline W^{(3)}\) describes a whole second-layer population, and \(W^{(2)}\) describes how population-level vectors are transported between the two layers.

Given the current state, define

\[
z^{(2)}=W^{(2)}\phi(z^{(1)}),
\]

\[
\delta^{(2)}
=
\overline W^{(3)}\odot\phi'(z^{(2)}),
\]

and

\[
r
=
\mathbb E\!\left[
\overline W^{(3)}\phi(z^{(2)})
\right]-1.
\]

The proposed continuous dynamics are

\[
\dot z^{(1)}
=
-2r\,
\phi'(z^{(1)})
\odot
\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*\delta^{(2)},
\]

\[
\dot W^{(2)}
=
-2r\,
\delta^{(2)}\otimes\phi(z^{(1)}),
\]

\[
\dot{\overline W}^{(3)}
=
-2r\,\phi(z^{(2)}).
\]

These are just forward propagation and backpropagation written for neuron populations. The symbol \(\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*\) is the limiting version of the finite matrix transpose \(\bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top\). The middle update is the population version of a rank-one outer-product update.

To prove that this is the right replacement, the first obligation is to derive these equations exactly from finite-width gradient flow. Otherwise they could simply be plausible equations whose loss happens to resemble the finite network’s loss. The proof differentiates the actual finite loss, includes all width-dependent learning-rate factors, and obtains the finite version of these equations without approximation. It uses an invertible change of the first-layer coordinate only to obtain estimates that do not deteriorate with width; this does not alter the underlying dynamics.

Next, one must specify what “the current population state” contains. The distributions of \(z^{(1)}\), \(z^{(2)}\), and \(\overline W^{(3)}\) are not enough. Two networks can have the same current hidden distributions and the same loss but different values of

\[
\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*\delta^{(2)},
\]

and therefore different next first-layer updates.

The limiting state consequently remembers the result of every fixed finite training computation built from

\[
W^{(2)},\qquad
\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*,\qquad
\phi,\qquad
\phi',
\]

and coordinatewise arithmetic. It records the population distributions, squared sizes, and correlations of those computations. One can view this as retaining a black-box description of \(W^{(2)}\): we do not retain all its entries, but we retain its answer to every forward or backward query that training can generate. This is what the proof calls the action law.

Once that state has been chosen, the next obligation is to show that the displayed equations can actually be run. Given one current action law, every term on the right must be defined, there must be a solution for some future interval, that solution must be unique, and it must not blow up later. In less formal language: the current state must have exactly one future, and small errors in the current state must not instantly produce huge errors.

Uniqueness is also what turns the equations into a genuinely autonomous or Markovian system. If two mathematical representations answer every training-relevant forward/backward query identically, then they have the same derivatives. Uniqueness then gives them the same future. Training can therefore be stopped at time \(s\), its past discarded, and restarted from the complete current action law. This is much stronger than constructing a family of fitted distributions indexed by time.

But a perfectly well-defined autonomous system might still have nothing to do with the finite network. The proof must next establish fidelity: exact finite training must approach this system. The central comparison is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{exact finite GD}
&\approx
\text{finite-width continuous gradient flow}\\
&\approx
\text{finite-width Euler approximation}\\
&\approx
\text{population Euler approximation}\\
&\approx
\text{continuum flow}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Each approximation has a distinct purpose, but they form one chain.

First, the proof obtains bounds that hold uniformly in \(n\). This matters because an error of size \(10^{-6}\) is useless if the dynamics can amplify it by a factor growing like \(n\). Uniform bounds show that the middle matrix cannot amplify vectors arbitrarily and that the finite-width vector field has a width-independent stability constant.

The proof then introduces an auxiliary mesh \(\delta\) and applies Euler’s method to the already continuous finite-width gradient flow. For fixed \(\delta\) and a fixed time interval \([0,T]\), there are only about \(T/\delta\) update steps. That is a fixed finite computation, so the tensor-program law of large numbers can identify its width limit.

There is one complication: the real finite Euler scheme feeds empirical averages back into later updates. The proof introduces a population oracle that replaces those empirical averages by their limiting population values. The tensor theorem identifies the oracle’s width limit, ordinary concentration makes the empirical-average errors vanish, and a repeated stability estimate shows that the real Euler scheme remains close to the oracle.

Finally, the uniform Euler error is \(O(\delta)\) at both finite and infinite width. Therefore one first fixes \(\delta\), lets \(n\to\infty\), and then lets \(\delta\to0\). This identifies the width limit of finite-width continuous gradient flow.

Separately, the actual GD step is denoted by \(\eta\). The proof estimates

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\operatorname{distance}
\left(
\text{GD}_{n,\eta}(t),
\text{GF}_n(t)
\right)
\le
C_T\left(
\eta+\eta\sqrt n+\eta^2n
\right).
\]

With the theorem’s prescribed choice

\[
\eta_n=n^{-2},
\]

this error vanishes. Combining the two comparisons proves that exact discrete GD approaches the autonomous continuum system.

Loss convergence is then a consequence, not the main definition of success. The proof first controls the complete action state and then separately checks that output, loss, hidden trajectories, tangent kernels, and mean-square velocities are continuous enough to inherit convergence. Some of these checks require extra tail estimates because backpropagated signals can be large even though \(\phi=\arctan\) is bounded.

This also clarifies the two limits. Let \(\mathcal S_{n,\eta}\) denote the complete training state at width \(n\) and step size \(\eta\). Taking the learning-rate limit first means

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\left(
\lim_{\eta\to0}\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
\right).
\]

For each fixed \(n\), discrete GD becomes finite-width continuous gradient flow; then the width tends to infinity. This order is meaningful and is supported by the proof.

Taking width first means

\[
\lim_{\eta\to0}
\left(
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
\right).
\]

The inner limit would be an infinite-width discrete-time training rule at fixed nonzero \(\eta\). That is also a meaningful question, but this document does not prove that the inner limit exists or that subsequently sending \(\eta\to0\) produces the same continuum flow.

The theorem itself proves a specified diagonal limit:

\[
\mathcal S_{n,\eta_n}\longrightarrow\mathcal S,
\qquad
\eta_n=n^{-2}.
\]

This means width grows and the step shrinks according to one prescribed relationship. It is weaker than an unrestricted joint limit, which would require convergence along every possible sequence

\[
n_k\to\infty,\qquad \eta_k\to0.
\]

The proved error contains \(\eta\sqrt n\), so it is not uniform over every such route. This does not show that the unrestricted joint limit fails; it only shows that this proof does not establish it.

Order dependence is easy to see in the scalar example

\[
a_{n,\eta}=\frac{n\eta}{1+n\eta}.
\]

Sending \(\eta\to0\) first gives \(0\), while sending \(n\to\infty\) first gives \(1\). Along \(\eta_n=1/n\), the value is always \(1/2\). Thus the two iterated limits and a diagonal can all describe different regimes.

The statement “a joint limit exists even though neither iterated limit exists” is also mathematically meaningful, provided “joint” means convergence along every simultaneous route. For example,

\[
c_{n,\eta}
=
\eta(-1)^n+\frac1n\sin(1/\eta)
\]

satisfies

\[
|c_{n,\eta}|\le \eta+\frac1n,
\]

so \(c_{n,\eta}\to0\) whenever \(n\to\infty\) and \(\eta\to0\) together. Yet for fixed \(\eta\), the \(n\)-limit oscillates, and for fixed \(n\), the \(\eta\)-limit oscillates. Thus neither iterated limit exists.

The last distinction is crucial: the auxiliary mesh \(\delta\) is not the physical GD step \(\eta\). Fixing \(\delta\), taking width to infinity, and then removing \(\delta\) is a proof technique for identifying the width limit of continuous gradient flow. The physical theorem is the diagonal statement \(\eta_n=n^{-2}\).

Your high-level picture is essentially right, with one correction:

\[
\boxed{\text{The limiting system is autonomous, but not finite-dimensional in the usual sense.}}
\]

It has a finite list of named evolving objects,

\[
z^{(1)},\qquad W^{(2)},\qquad \overline W^{(3)},
\]

and finitely many evolution equations. But \(z^{(1)}\) and \(\overline W^{(3)}\) describe whole neuron populations, while \(W^{(2)}\) acts on infinitely many possible population-level probes. So the accurate description is:

\[
\boxed{\text{a closed, autonomous, infinite-dimensional action-law flow with finitely many equations.}}
\]

## What the candidate limiting system is

At the population level, define

\[
z^{(2)}
=
W^{(2)}\phi(z^{(1)}),
\]

\[
\delta^{(2)}
=
\overline W^{(3)}
\odot\phi'(z^{(2)}),
\]

and

\[
r
=
\mathbb E_2\!\left[
\overline W^{(3)}\phi(z^{(2)})
\right]-1.
\]

Here \(\mathbb E_1\) and \(\mathbb E_2\) mean population averages over first- and second-layer neurons, respectively.

The proposed continuum equations are

\[
\frac{d}{dt}z^{(1)}
=
-2r\,
\phi'(z^{(1)})
\odot
\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*
\delta^{(2)},
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}W^{(2)}
=
-2r\,
\delta^{(2)}\otimes\phi(z^{(1)}),
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\overline W^{(3)}
=
-2r\,\phi(z^{(2)}).
\]

The rank-one operator in the middle equation means

\[
\left(
\delta^{(2)}\otimes\phi(z^{(1)})
\right)v
=
\delta^{(2)}
\,
\mathbb E_1\!\left[
\phi(z^{(1)})v
\right].
\]

At finite width, \(\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*\) is simply \(\bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top\).

The theorem’s goal is not merely to show that a curve satisfying these equations can be written down. It must prove three logically separate facts:

1. These equations define a genuine autonomous dynamical system.
2. Exact finite-width, finite-step GD converges to that system.
3. Important observables such as loss, kernels, and hidden paths converge as consequences of state convergence.

None of these three facts alone implies the other two.

## The technical obligations

### 1. Derive the candidate equations exactly

The continuum equations cannot simply be guessed from a limiting loss curve.

One begins with the finite-width loss, differentiates it with respect to every weight, includes the width-dependent layer multipliers, and obtains the finite-width gradient-flow equations exactly.

The document introduces one invertible coordinate change for \(z^{(1)}\) to obtain uniform estimates, but that is an exact change of variables, not a linearization.

This obligation establishes that the proposed vector field genuinely comes from the original scaled gradient descent.

### 2. Define a state rich enough to determine the future

The marginal distributions of

\[
z^{(1)},\qquad z^{(2)},\qquad \overline W^{(3)}
\]

are not sufficient. The next derivative of \(z^{(1)}\) requires

\[
\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*\delta^{(2)},
\]

which is not determined by those marginal distributions.

The state must therefore retain every fixed finite forward/backward computation generated using

\[
W^{(2)},\qquad
\bigl(W^{(2)}\bigr)^*,\qquad
\phi,\qquad
\phi',
\]

together with coordinatewise arithmetic, joint empirical laws, and normalized inner products.

This collection is the action law. A uniform bound on how strongly \(W^{(2)}\) can amplify vectors is also required.

Without this step, the proposed “state” could omit information that changes its own future.

### 3. Construct the limiting initial action

The matrices \(W_n^{(2)}(0)\) have changing dimensions, so they cannot converge entry by entry to a fixed matrix.

Instead, one must construct the limits of all finite recipes such as

\[
W_n^{(2)}v_n,
\qquad
\bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top u_n,
\qquad
W_n^{(2)}
\phi'\!\left(
\bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top u_n
\right).
\]

The limiting joint laws must be mutually consistent. One must also prove that the limiting backward operation really is the transpose-like operation corresponding to the same forward \(W^{(2)}\), not multiplication by a fresh independent Gaussian matrix.

This reused-transpose dependence is one of the main technical difficulties.

### 4. Prove internal well-posedness

Writing

\[
\dot{\text{state}}=V(\text{state})
\]

does not yet produce a dynamical system.

One must prove:

- every term in \(V\) is defined;
- local solutions exist;
- solutions are unique;
- solutions depend continuously on the current state;
- no finite-time blow-up occurs.

The proof obtains local existence and uniqueness from a Lipschitz/contraction argument. It obtains global continuation from norm estimates and the loss-dissipation identity

\[
\frac{d}{dt}L(t)
=
-4r(t)^2K(t)
\le0.
\]

Thus the candidate is an actual solution of a differential equation, not merely a time-indexed family of fitted probability laws.

### 5. Prove closure and restartability

Even uniqueness on one chosen mathematical representation is not enough. Different representations may encode the same action law.

One must prove:

> If two current states give identical answers to every finite forward/backward probe, then their vector fields also give identical answers to every probe.

Uniqueness then implies that their future action laws remain identical.

If \(\Phi_t\) denotes evolution for time \(t\), this gives

\[
\Phi_t\!\left(\Phi_s(\text{current action law})\right)
=
\Phi_{t+s}(\text{current action law}).
\]

This is the precise deterministic Markov property. The full action law is Markovian; the scalar loss and the marginal hidden distributions generally are not.

### 6. Obtain estimates uniform in width

A finite-width ODE may be perfectly well posed for each \(n\) while its stability constant explodes as \(n\to\infty\).

The proof therefore needs width-independent bounds on quantities such as

\[
\|W_n^{(2)}(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\]

and a width-independent Lipschitz estimate for the finite-width vector field.

These estimates ensure that:

- small errors are not amplified uncontrollably as \(n\to\infty\);
- Euler approximation errors are \(O(\delta)\) uniformly in \(n\);
- finite-width trajectories remain in a common bounded region.

This uniformity is the bridge between finite-dimensional ODE theory and the width limit.

### 7. Identify the width limit

There are two standard strategies for this kind of problem:

\[
\text{compactness}
\;+\;
\text{identify every subsequential limit}
\;+\;
\text{uniqueness},
\]

or a direct coupling showing that finite and limiting systems are close.

This proof uses a direct coupling. It introduces an auxiliary time mesh \(\delta>0\) and compares

\[
\text{finite-width continuous flow}
\]

to

\[
\text{finite-width Euler at mesh }\delta,
\]

then to a finite-width population oracle, then to continuum Euler, and finally to the continuum flow:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{finite-width flow}
&\approx
\text{finite-width Euler}_{\delta}\\
&\approx
\text{population oracle}_{n,\delta}\\
&\longrightarrow
\text{continuum Euler}_{\delta}\\
&\approx
\text{continuum flow}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

The oracle replaces empirical scalar feedback terms with their deterministic continuum values. The differences are explicit empirical Gram errors, controlled by a tensor-program theorem and discrete Gronwall.

### 8. Compare exact discrete GD with finite-width gradient flow

This is the gradient-flow limit.

Let \(\eta\) denote the actual base GD step. The proof obtains, schematically,

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
d\!\left(
\text{exact GD}_{n,\eta}(t),
\text{finite-width GF}_n(t)
\right)
\le
C_T
\left(
\eta+\eta\sqrt n+\eta^2n
\right).
\]

For the theorem’s prescribed step

\[
\eta_n=n^{-2},
\]

the right side tends to zero.

Combining this with the width limit of the finite-width gradient flow gives

\[
\text{exact GD}_{n,\eta_n}
\longrightarrow
\text{continuum action flow}.
\]

### 9. Transfer convergence to observables

Loss convergence is weaker than state convergence. Two states can have the same loss now and different future derivatives.

Conversely, structural action-law convergence does not automatically imply convergence of every unbounded quantity. The proof separately establishes:

- output and loss convergence;
- path-law convergence for \(z^{(1)}(\cdot)\) and \(z^{(2)}(\cdot)\);
- tangent-kernel convergence;
- mean-square velocity convergence.

The last two require additional tail estimates because backpropagated signals are not uniformly bounded.

## The two physical limits

Let

\[
\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
\]

denote the complete exact-GD action state for width \(n\) and base step \(\eta\).

There are four different limit statements one might make.

### Learning-rate first, then width

First fix \(n\) and send \(\eta\downarrow0\):

\[
\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
=
\mathcal S_n^{\mathrm{GF}}.
\]

This produces finite-width continuous gradient flow.

Then send \(n\to\infty\):

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\mathcal S_n^{\mathrm{GF}}
=
\mathcal S.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\left(
\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
\right)
=
\mathcal S.
}
\]

This order is mathematically meaningful and is supported by the proof.

### Width first, then learning rate

First fix a nonzero \(\eta\) and ask whether

\[
\mathcal S_{\infty,\eta}
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
\]

exists.

If it does, \(\mathcal S_{\infty,\eta}\) is an infinite-width discrete-time recurrence, not yet a gradient flow. One would then ask whether

\[
\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}
\mathcal S_{\infty,\eta}
=
\mathcal S.
\]

This order is perfectly meaningful, but it is not proved in this document. Establishing it would require width estimates appropriate to fixed nonzero \(\eta\).

### A specified diagonal limit

Choose one schedule \(\eta=\eta_n\) and take both limits simultaneously:

\[
\mathcal S_{n,\eta_n}\longrightarrow\mathcal S.
\]

The theorem proves the particular diagonal

\[
\boxed{\eta_n=n^{-2}.}
\]

A diagonal statement only concerns that schedule. It does not automatically say what happens for \(\eta_n=n^{-1}\), \(\eta_n=n^{-1/2}\), or any other route.

### An unrestricted joint limit

The strongest statement would be

\[
\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\\eta\downarrow0}}
\mathcal S_{n,\eta}
=
\mathcal S.
\]

This means convergence along every sequence

\[
n_k\to\infty,\qquad \eta_k\downarrow0.
\]

Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) and all sufficiently small \(\eta\) must give a state within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\mathcal S\).

The document does not prove this unrestricted joint limit. Its GD-versus-GF estimate contains

\[
\eta\sqrt n,
\]

which is not small along every route to \(n=\infty,\eta=0\). This does not prove that the unrestricted joint limit fails; it means the available estimate is not uniform enough to establish it.

## Why order can matter

Consider the scalar example

\[
a_{n,\eta}
=
\frac{n\eta}{1+n\eta}.
\]

Learning-rate first gives

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\left(
\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}a_{n,\eta}
\right)
=0.
\]

Width first gives

\[
\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}
\left(
\lim_{n\to\infty}a_{n,\eta}
\right)
=1.
\]

Different diagonals also give different answers:

\[
\eta_n=n^{-2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a_{n,\eta_n}\to0,
\]

\[
\eta_n=n^{-1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a_{n,\eta_n}\to\frac12,
\]

\[
\eta_n=n^{-1/2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a_{n,\eta_n}\to1.
\]

This is what nonuniform interaction between the two parameters looks like.

Even agreement of both iterated limits does not guarantee an unrestricted joint limit. For

\[
b_{n,\eta}
=
\frac{n\eta}{1+(n\eta)^2},
\]

both iterated limits equal \(0\), but

\[
b_{n,1/n}=\frac12.
\]

## Can a joint limit exist when neither iterated limit exists?

Yes—provided “joint” means the unrestricted two-parameter limit. The sentence is mathematically well defined.

For example, let

\[
c_{n,\eta}
=
\eta(-1)^n
+
\frac1n\sin\!\left(\frac1\eta\right).
\]

Because

\[
|c_{n,\eta}|
\le
\eta+\frac1n,
\]

we have

\[
c_{n,\eta}\longrightarrow0
\]

along every route with \(n\to\infty\) and \(\eta\downarrow0\).

But for fixed \(\eta>0\), the \(n\)-limit fails because of \(\eta(-1)^n\). For fixed \(n\), the \(\eta\)-limit fails because of \(n^{-1}\sin(1/\eta)\). Thus neither iterated construction is defined, despite the unrestricted joint limit existing.

The final nuance is that the auxiliary mesh \(\delta\) in the proof is not the physical learning rate \(\eta\). The proof fixes \(\delta\), takes \(n\to\infty\), and then sends \(\delta\downarrow0\) only because the tensor-program theorem applies to a fixed finite number of Euler operations. Separately, it compares actual GD with step \(\eta_n=n^{-2}\) to finite-width gradient flow.

So the document proves:

\[
\boxed{
\text{a prescribed physical diagonal limit }
\eta_n=n^{-2},
}
\]

using

\[
\boxed{
\text{an auxiliary proof order }
\delta\text{ fixed}\;\to\;n\to\infty\;\to\;\delta\downarrow0.
}
\]

Those are related but logically different limit procedures.

We restart with one question:

> As both hidden layers become infinitely wide, what does the entire exact GD training process converge to, and does that limit still perform genuine nonlinear feature learning?

## 1. The finite-width system

There is one input \(x=1\) and one target \(y=1\). Both hidden layers have width \(n\). The activation is

\[
\phi(s)=\arctan(s).
\]

Because \(x=1\), the first-layer preactivation equals its weight:

\[
z_{n,i}^{(1)}=W_{n,i}^{(1)},\qquad 1\le i\le n.
\]

The second-layer preactivation is

\[
z_{n,j}^{(2)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
W_{n,ji}^{(2)}
\phi\!\left(z_{n,i}^{(1)}\right),
\qquad 1\le j\le n.
\]

The scalar output is

\[
f_n
=
\sum_{j=1}^n
W_{n,j}^{(3)}
\phi\!\left(z_{n,j}^{(2)}\right),
\]

and the loss is

\[
L_n=(f_n-1)^2.
\]

The independent initialization is

\[
W_{n,i}^{(1)}(0)\sim N(0,1),
\]

\[
W_{n,ji}^{(2)}(0)\sim N\!\left(0,\frac1n\right),
\]

\[
W_{n,j}^{(3)}(0)\sim N\!\left(0,\frac1{n^4}\right).
\]

Thus \(z^{(1)}\) and \(z^{(2)}\) are order-one quantities, while the initial output tends to zero:

\[
f_n(0)\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
L_n(0)\longrightarrow1.
\]

Gradient descent uses

\[
W_n^{(\ell)}(k+1)
=
W_n^{(\ell)}(k)
-
\eta_n\lambda_{\ell,n}
\nabla_{W_n^{(\ell)}}L_n(k),
\]

where

\[
\eta_n=n^{-2}
\]

and

\[
\lambda_{1,n}=n,\qquad
\lambda_{2,n}=1,\qquad
\lambda_{3,n}=n^{-1}.
\]

Macroscopic time is

\[
t=k\eta_n=\frac{k}{n^2}.
\]

Therefore, reaching a fixed time \(t\) requires approximately \(tn^2\) GD iterations. The theorem takes the width limit and the small-step limit together.

It is useful to rescale only the output weights:

\[
\overline W_{n,j}^{(3)}
=
nW_{n,j}^{(3)}.
\]

Then

\[
f_n
=
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
\overline W_{n,j}^{(3)}
\phi\!\left(z_{n,j}^{(2)}\right).
\]

## 2. The primary objective: identify the entire limiting dynamics

The main objective is to construct a unique deterministic law-level evolution

\[
\left(
z^{(1)}(t),
W^{(2)}(t),
\overline W^{(3)}(t)
\right),
\qquad t\ge0,
\]

that faithfully describes exact finite-width GD as \(n\to\infty\).

Here “deterministic law-level evolution” means that the limiting population distributions and correlations are deterministic. A representative neuron remains a random variable because different neurons have different initial labels, but the distribution of those labels and their evolution no longer depend on the particular finite-width random sample.

The desired convergence is

\[
\boxed{
\text{exact discrete GD at width }n
\longrightarrow
\text{one unique continuous-time population evolution}.
}
\]

This must hold:

- along the full sequence \(n\to\infty\), not merely a subsequence;
- in probability over the random initialization;
- uniformly for \(0\le t\le T\), for every fixed \(T<\infty\);
- for the hidden representations and matrix-mediated backpropagation, not only for \(f_n(t)\).

## 3. What convergence of the complete state means

The matrix \(W_n^{(2)}\) changes dimension with \(n\), so its entries cannot converge to the entries of one fixed matrix. Instead, the theorem tests every fixed finite computation that training can perform with \(W_n^{(2)}\).

A first-layer probe is a vector indexed by first-layer neurons. Denote such probes by

\[
v_n^1,\ldots,v_n^m\in\mathbb R^n.
\]

A second-layer probe is a vector indexed by second-layer neurons. Denote these by

\[
u_n^1,\ldots,u_n^r\in\mathbb R^n.
\]

Starting with \(z_n^{(1)}\) and \(\overline W_n^{(3)}\), probes are generated using:

\[
\phi,\quad \phi',\quad
\text{coordinatewise arithmetic},
\]

\[
v_n\longmapsto W_n^{(2)}v_n,
\]

and

\[
u_n\longmapsto
\bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top u_n.
\]

For example, training uses the sequence

\[
v_n^0=\phi(z_n^{(1)}),
\]

\[
u_n^0=W_n^{(2)}v_n^0=z_n^{(2)},
\]

\[
u_n^1
=
\overline W_n^{(3)}
\odot\phi'(z_n^{(2)}),
\]

\[
v_n^1
=
\bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top u_n^1.
\]

Here \(\odot\) denotes coordinatewise multiplication.

For every fixed finite list of first-layer probes, the theorem requires

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi\!\left(
v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)
\right)
-
\mathbb E\,
\psi\!\left(
V^1(t),\ldots,V^m(t)
\right)
\right|
\longrightarrow0
\]

in probability, for every bounded continuous test function \(\psi\). Second moments must converge as well.

Separately, for every fixed finite list of second-layer probes,

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
\chi\!\left(
u_{n,j}^1(t),\ldots,u_{n,j}^r(t)
\right)
-
\mathbb E\,
\chi\!\left(
U^1(t),\ldots,U^r(t)
\right)
\right|
\longrightarrow0
\]

in probability, again together with second moments.

All normalized same-layer inner products must also converge:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
v_{n,i}(t)\widetilde v_{n,i}(t)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E[V(t)\widetilde V(t)],
\]

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
u_{n,j}(t)\widetilde u_{n,j}(t)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E[U(t)\widetilde U(t)].
\]

Finally, the matrix action must remain uniformly bounded:

\[
\|W_n^{(2)}(t)v\|_n
\le M_T\|v\|_n
\]

for all \(v\), uniformly over \(0\le t\le T\), with probability tending to one.

Together, these conditions mean:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Every fixed finite forward/backward computation performed by training
has a deterministic limit.}
}
\]

This is the document’s precise “action-law convergence.”

## 4. The closure objective

Convergence alone is insufficient. The limiting information must determine its own future.

The current limiting state contains:

- the first-layer population data;
- the second-layer population data;
- how \(W^{(2)}\) sends every training-relevant first-layer probe forward;
- how \((W^{(2)})^\top\) sends every training-relevant second-layer probe backward;
- the joint laws and inner products of all these quantities.

The training equations use only these operations. Therefore the current action law determines the current velocity. Uniqueness then determines the entire future.

If \(\Phi_t\) denotes evolution for time \(t\), restartability means

\[
\Phi_t\!\left(\Phi_s(\text{current action law})\right)
=
\Phi_{t+s}(\text{current action law}).
\]

No initialization array or previous trajectory must be retained as hidden memory.

## 5. The observable convergence objective

The theorem also requires convergence of complete neuron trajectories, not just distributions at one time.

For the first hidden layer, define

\[
\Lambda_n^{(1)}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\delta_{z_{n,i}^{(1)}(\cdot)}.
\]

This is the empirical distribution of the entire paths

\[
t\longmapsto z_{n,i}^{(1)}(t).
\]

Similarly,

\[
\Lambda_n^{(2)}
=
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
\delta_{z_{n,j}^{(2)}(\cdot)}.
\]

The theorem proves

\[
\Lambda_n^{(1)}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal L\!\left(z^{(1)}(\cdot)\right),
\]

\[
\Lambda_n^{(2)}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal L\!\left(z^{(2)}(\cdot)\right)
\]

in path-space \(W_2\). Concretely, this means convergence of the path distributions together with convergence of their mean squared maximum sizes. It retains temporal correlations: how a neuron’s value at one time relates to its value later.

The output and loss also converge uniformly:

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|f_n(t)-f(t)|
\longrightarrow0,
\]

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|L_n(t)-L(t)|
\longrightarrow0
\]

in probability.

## 6. The nondegeneracy objective

A mathematically existing limit could still be uninteresting. For example, only \(W^{(3)}\) might learn while both hidden layers remain frozen.

The theorem must therefore prove that both hidden representations move. For sufficiently small \(T>0\),

\[
\int_0^T
\mathbb E
\left|
\frac{d}{dt}z^{(1)}(t)
\right|^2dt
>0,
\]

\[
\int_0^T
\mathbb E
\left|
\frac{d}{dt}z^{(2)}(t)
\right|^2dt
>0.
\]

It also proves actual nonzero displacement:

\[
\mathbb E
\left|
z^{(1)}(T)-z^{(1)}(0)
\right|^2>0,
\]

\[
\mathbb E
\left|
z^{(2)}(T)-z^{(2)}(0)
\right|^2>0.
\]

Velocity energy rules out “it moves only at an isolated instant.” Displacement rules out “it moves but returns exactly to where it started.”

## 7. The kernel criterion for all three layers

Define the scaled contribution of layer \(\ell\) to the tangent kernel by

\[
K_n^{(\ell)}
=
\lambda_{\ell,n}
\sum_{\alpha\in W_n^{(\ell)}}
\left(
\frac{\partial f_n}
{\partial W_{n,\alpha}^{(\ell)}}
\right)^2.
\]

The total scaled kernel is

\[
K_n
=
K_n^{(1)}+K_n^{(2)}+K_n^{(3)}.
\]

For the continuous gradient flow,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}f_n
=
-2(f_n-1)K_n
\]

and therefore

\[
\frac{d}{dt}L_n
=
-4(f_n-1)^2K_n.
\]

Thus \(K_n^{(\ell)}\) measures how strongly layer \(\ell\) contributes to the instantaneous decrease of the loss.

The theorem proves convergence of all three blocks and, for sufficiently small \(T>0\),

\[
\int_0^T K^{(\ell)}(t)\,dt>0,
\qquad \ell=1,2,3.
\]

It also proves that

\[
K(t)
\]

is not constant. This distinguishes the limit from a frozen tangent-kernel regime.

## 8. The genuine-nonlinearity criterion

Movement alone does not guarantee nonlinear feature learning. The hidden variables could move only inside a regime where \(\phi\) behaves effectively like an affine function.

For each hidden layer \(\ell=1,2\), define

\[
\mathcal N^{(\ell)}(t)
=
\inf_{a,b\in\mathbb R}
\mathbb E
\left[
\left(
\phi(z^{(\ell)}(t))
-a-bz^{(\ell)}(t)
\right)^2
\right].
\]

This is the smallest mean-square error obtained by approximating the activation with an affine function of the preactivation.

The theorem proves, for sufficiently small time,

\[
\mathcal N^{(1)}(t)>0,
\qquad
\mathcal N^{(2)}(t)>0.
\]

Therefore neither hidden activation has collapsed to an affine transformation under its evolving population distribution.

The main objective is consequently the conjunction of three claims:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}
\textbf{Fidelity:}&
\text{exact finite-width GD converges to the proposed law-level dynamics};\\[1mm]
\textbf{Closure:}&
\text{the current limiting action law uniquely determines its future};\\[1mm]
\textbf{Nondegeneracy:}&
\text{both hidden layers move, all layers affect learning, and }\phi
\text{ remains nonlinear}.
\end{array}
}
\]

This is not a theorem about eventual global optimization. It does not prove \(L(t)\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\). It is a rigorous finite-time theorem identifying the true infinite-width training dynamics and proving that those dynamics are genuinely nonlinear and feature-learning.

My displayed equation showed only the first-layer condition. The complete criterion requires two separate families of convergence statements.

Let

\[
v_n^1(t),\ldots,v_n^m(t)\in\mathbb R^n
\]

be first-layer probes, indexed by first-layer neurons \(i\). Let

\[
u_n^1(t),\ldots,u_n^r(t)\in\mathbb R^n
\]

be second-layer probes, indexed by second-layer neurons \(j\).

They are connected by

\[
v_n\longmapsto W_n^{(2)}v_n,
\]

which produces a second-layer probe, and

\[
u_n\longmapsto \bigl(W_n^{(2)}\bigr)^\top u_n,
\]

which produces a first-layer probe.

For every finite list of first-layer probes and every bounded continuous test function \(\psi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\), the requirement is

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi\!\left(
v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)
\right)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\,
\psi\!\left(
V^1(t),\ldots,V^m(t)
\right).
\]

Separately, for every finite list of second-layer probes and every bounded continuous \(\chi:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\),

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
\chi\!\left(
u_{n,j}^1(t),\ldots,u_{n,j}^r(t)
\right)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\,
\chi\!\left(
U^1(t),\ldots,U^r(t)
\right).
\]

Both statements hold uniformly for \(0\le t\le T\), in probability. To obtain \(W_2\), rather than merely weak convergence, the corresponding second moments must also converge:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a=1}^m
|v_{n,i}^a(t)|^2
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\sum_{a=1}^m|V^a(t)|^2,
\]

and

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{b=1}^r
|u_{n,j}^b(t)|^2
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\sum_{b=1}^r|U^b(t)|^2.
\]

Same-layer inner products are also recorded:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
v_{n,i}\widetilde v_{n,i}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E[V\widetilde V],
\]

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
u_{n,j}\widetilde u_{n,j}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E[U\widetilde U].
\]

There is generally no empirical joint law of the form

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{(v_{n,i},u_{n,i})}.
\]

Although both layers happen to have width \(n\), index \(i\) in the first layer and index \(j\) in the second layer label different neuron populations. Pairing first-layer neuron \(i\) with second-layer neuron \(i\) would be arbitrary and would change under separate neuron relabelings.

Instead, cross-layer dependence is recorded through \(W_n^{(2)}\). For example, these are legitimate same-layer joint laws:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
\delta_{\left(u_{n,j},\,(W_n^{(2)}v_n)_j\right)}
\]

on the second layer, and

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\delta_{\left(v_{n,i},\,((W_n^{(2)})^\top u_n)_i\right)}
\]

on the first layer.

Cross-layer scalar interactions are likewise captured by the adjoint identity

\[
\frac1n
u_n^\top W_n^{(2)}v_n
=
\frac1n
\left((W_n^{(2)})^\top u_n\right)^\top v_n.
\]

The left side is a second-layer inner product; the right side is the identical quantity expressed as a first-layer inner product.

Thus the complete criterion is

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{l}
\text{joint-law and second-moment convergence for every finite list of}\\
\text{first-layer probes }v;\\[1mm]
\text{the same convergence for every finite list of second-layer probes }u;\\[1mm]
\text{with the two families connected by }W^{(2)}\text{ and }(W^{(2)})^\top.
\end{array}}
\]

The proof states this as “same-side probe tuples” in [lines 484–487](/tmp/L2_FULL_AUDITED_PROOF.md:484). “Same-side” means separately within the first-layer and second-layer populations—not only the \(v\)-side.

items.text: I’m rebuilding the action-law explanation from finite vectors and ordinary matrix multiplication only. The functional-analysis language will appear only as a final translation; the actual criterion can be understood through concrete “computational recipes,” empirical averages, and matrix transposes.

At every finite width, there are only vectors, matrices, sums, and ordinary probability distributions. The functional-analysis language is packaging for what happens when the vector length \(n\) tends to infinity.

Let

\[
W=W^{(2)}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}
\]

be the weights between the two hidden layers. Forward propagation uses

\[
z^{(2)}=W\phi(z^{(1)}).
\]

Backpropagation first forms

\[
\delta^{(2)}
=
\overline W^{(3)}\odot\phi'(z^{(2)}),
\]

where \(\odot\) means coordinatewise multiplication, and then sends it backward through

\[
W^\top\delta^{(2)}.
\]

The first-layer velocity is

\[
\frac{d}{dt}z^{(1)}
=
-2r\,
\phi'(z^{(1)})\odot
W^\top\delta^{(2)},
\]

where \(r=f-1\) is the output error.

So training queries the same matrix in two directions:

\[
\text{forward: }v\mapsto Wv,
\qquad
\text{backward: }u\mapsto W^\top u.
\]

## Why marginal distributions are insufficient

Suppose

\[
a=\phi(z^{(1)})=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
d=\delta^{(2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Consider

\[
W_{\mathrm I}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
W_{\mathrm{II}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Their forward actions agree:

\[
W_{\mathrm I}a
=
W_{\mathrm{II}}a
=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore both networks can have exactly the same current first-layer activations and exactly the same second-layer preactivations.

But their backward actions differ:

\[
W_{\mathrm I}^{\top}d
=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
W_{\mathrm{II}}^{\top}d
=
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence their next first-layer velocities differ.

This proves the substantive point:

\[
\boxed{
\text{The current distributions of }z^{(1)}\text{ and }z^{(2)}
\text{ do not determine the future.}
}
\]

The state must also retain enough information about how \(W\) and \(W^\top\) act on the vectors produced during training.

## What “retain the action” means

Think of a probe as a finite computational recipe. A probe may perform operations such as:

1. Start with \(z^{(1)}\) or \(\overline W^{(3)}\).
2. Apply \(\phi\) or \(\phi'\) coordinatewise.
3. Add or multiply vectors coordinatewise.
4. Send a first-layer vector forward using \(W\).
5. Send a second-layer vector backward using \(W^\top\).
6. Repeat these operations a fixed finite number of times.
7. Measure empirical distributions or normalized dot products.

For example:

\[
v_0=\phi(z^{(1)}),
\]

\[
u_0=Wv_0=z^{(2)},
\]

\[
u_1=\overline W^{(3)}\odot\phi'(u_0)
=\delta^{(2)},
\]

\[
v_1=W^\top u_1,
\]

\[
v_2=\phi'(z^{(1)})\odot v_1,
\]

\[
u_2=Wv_2.
\]

Here \(v_0,v_1,v_2\) are first-layer vectors, while \(u_0,u_1,u_2\) are second-layer vectors. A probe can continue nesting these operations, but every individual probe must contain only finitely many steps.

## The exact convergence criterion

Take any fixed finite collection of first-layer probes

\[
v_n^1(t),\ldots,v_n^m(t)\in\mathbb R^n.
\]

Their empirical joint distribution is the distribution obtained by selecting a neuron index \(i\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and observing

\[
\bigl(v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)\bigr).
\]

Written as a probability measure, it is

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\delta_{\left(v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)\right)}.
\]

Convergence means that for every reasonable continuous test function \(\psi\),

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\psi\!\left(
v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)
\right)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\,
\psi\!\left(V^1(t),\ldots,V^m(t)\right).
\]

The limiting random variables \(V^1,\ldots,V^m\) describe the limiting population statistics of those probes.

Second moments must also converge:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
|v_{n,i}^k(t)|^2
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E|V^k(t)|^2.
\]

This prevents a small number of extremely large coordinates from being invisible to the limiting distribution. Weak distributional convergence together with this second-moment control is what the proof calls \(W_2\) convergence.

The identical condition is imposed on every finite collection of second-layer probes.

The proof also explicitly tracks normalized dot products:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
v_{n,i}(t)\widetilde v_{n,i}(t)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\!\left[
V(t)\widetilde V(t)
\right],
\]

and, for second-layer probes,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
u_{n,j}(t)\widetilde u_{n,j}(t)
\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\!\left[
U(t)\widetilde U(t)
\right].
\]

These dot products record angles, correlations, and squared sizes. They are essential because the rank-one weight update contains precisely such quantities after repeated time steps.

The convergence must hold uniformly over time. For every fixed probe statistic \(Q_n(t)\), limiting statistic \(Q(t)\), finite \(T\), and \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\left(
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
|Q_n(t)-Q(t)|>\varepsilon
\right)
\longrightarrow0.
\]

## Packaging all probes into one criterion

There are infinitely many possible finite recipes. The proof lists them as

\[
R_1,R_2,R_3,\ldots
\]

and lets \(\operatorname{error}(R_k)\) measure the disagreement on recipe \(R_k\). It then defines

\[
d_{\mathrm{action}}
=
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}
2^{-k}
\min\left\{1,\operatorname{error}(R_k)\right\}.
\]

The weights \(2^{-k}\) make the infinite sum finite. Mathematically,

\[
d_{\mathrm{action}}\to0
\]

is equivalent to saying:

> For every fixed finite recipe, its empirical joint laws, second moments, and dot products converge to the corresponding limiting quantities.

The theorem proves

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
d_{\mathrm{action}}
\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{in probability}.
\]

This is the precise meaning of convergence of the matrix action.

## One additional boundedness requirement

Finite probes alone could miss a direction on which \(W\) becomes enormous. The proof therefore also requires a uniform amplification bound:

\[
\|Wv\|_n\le M_T\|v\|_n
\]

for every vector \(v\), with high probability, uniformly over width and \(0\le t\le T\). Here

\[
\|v\|_n^2=\frac1n\sum_i v_i^2.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}
=
\sup_{v\ne0}
\frac{\|Wv\|_n}{\|v\|_n}
\le M_T.
\]

This rules out uncontrolled amplification hiding outside the finitely inspected probes.

## Why this determines the future

Every term in the training equations is itself one of these finite recipes:

\[
z^{(2)}=W\phi(z^{(1)}),
\]

\[
\delta^{(2)}
=
\overline W^{(3)}\odot\phi'(z^{(2)}),
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}z^{(1)}
=
-2r\,\phi'(z^{(1)})\odot W^\top\delta^{(2)},
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}W
=
-\frac{2r}{n}\,
\delta^{(2)}\phi(z^{(1)})^\top.
\]

Therefore, if two limiting states give the same answer to every finite probe, they give the same current velocities. After a short time, their new states again give the same probe answers. Repeating this argument determines the whole future.

The limit does not retain every imaginable action of \(W\). It retains only its action on vectors reachable from the current neural-network variables through forward propagation, backpropagation, coordinatewise nonlinearities, and their finite repetitions. Any direction that can never be reached by these operations can never affect training and is discarded.

This is what the proof calls the current cyclic space. The “Hilbert spaces” are simply a rigorous home for all limiting probe vectors, their dot products, and the two operations corresponding to \(W\) and \(W^\top\).

Yes. It is written precisely in Sections 4.2 and 5.3. The criterion is not operator-norm convergence of the matrices \(W_n^{(2)}\). It is convergence of every finite observable generated by repeatedly applying \(W_n^{(2)}\) and \((W_n^{(2)})^*\).

Let

\[
\mathcal H_1=L^2(\Omega_1),\qquad
\mathcal H_2=L^2(\Omega_2)
\]

represent the first- and second-layer populations. In the limit,

\[
W^{(2)}:\mathcal H_1\to\mathcal H_2,
\qquad
(W^{(2)})^*:\mathcal H_2\to\mathcal H_1.
\]

A first-layer quantity is an element of \(\mathcal H_1\); a second-layer quantity is an element of \(\mathcal H_2\). They cannot be placed in the same coordinatewise joint distribution because their neuron indices belong to different populations.

Starting with \(z^{(1)}\) and the rescaled output weights \(\overline W^{(3)}\), construct probes recursively:

\[
v\in\mathcal H_1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
W^{(2)}v\in\mathcal H_2,
\]

\[
u\in\mathcal H_2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(W^{(2)})^*u\in\mathcal H_1.
\]

At either layer, one may also apply the required coordinatewise functions, such as \(\phi,\phi'\), products occurring in backpropagation, and finite linear combinations.

For example, the following are successive probes:

\[
\phi(z^{(1)})\in\mathcal H_1,
\]

\[
z^{(2)}
=
W^{(2)}\phi(z^{(1)})
\in\mathcal H_2,
\]

\[
\delta^{(2)}
=
\overline W^{(3)}\phi'(z^{(2)})
\in\mathcal H_2,
\]

\[
(W^{(2)})^*\delta^{(2)}
\in\mathcal H_1,
\]

\[
W^{(2)}
\left[
\phi'(z^{(1)})(W^{(2)})^*\delta^{(2)}
\right]
\in\mathcal H_2.
\]

The construction allows every finite nesting of this kind.

For any finite list of first-layer probes \(v^1,\ldots,v^m\), the finite-width empirical joint law is

\[
\mu_{n,t}^{v^1,\ldots,v^m}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\delta_{
\left(
v_{n,i}^1(t),\ldots,v_{n,i}^m(t)
\right)
}.
\]

The criterion requires

\[
\mu_{n,t}^{v^1,\ldots,v^m}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal L\bigl(v^1(t),\ldots,v^m(t)\bigr)
\]

in \(W_2(\mathbb R^m)\), uniformly in \(t\in[0,T]\), in probability.

There is an identical requirement for every finite list of second-layer probes. In addition, all same-layer inner products must converge:

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
v_{n,i}(t)\widetilde v_{n,i}(t)
\longrightarrow
\langle v(t),\widetilde v(t)\rangle_{\mathcal H_1},
\]

and

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n
u_{n,j}(t)\widetilde u_{n,j}(t)
\longrightarrow
\langle u(t),\widetilde u(t)\rangle_{\mathcal H_2}.
\]

A finite collection of these joint laws and inner products is called a record. If \(d_R\) measures the difference between two states on record \(R\), the proof enumerates all finite records \(R_1,R_2,\ldots\) and defines

\[
d_{\mathrm{act}}
=
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}
2^{-k}
\left(1\wedge d_{R_k}\right).
\]

Therefore,

\[
d_{\mathrm{act}}\to0
\]

means that every fixed finite nested forward/backward computation has the correct limiting joint law and inner products. This is defined explicitly in [equations (5.12)–(5.13)](/tmp/L2_FULL_AUDITED_PROOF.md:476).

The main convergence statement is

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
d_{\mathrm{act}}\bigl(
\text{width-}n\text{ state at }t,
\text{limiting state at }t
\bigr)
\longrightarrow0
\]

in probability. This is proved at [equation (5.18)](/tmp/L2_FULL_AUDITED_PROOF.md:541).

There is also an equivalent basis-free criterion. Two limiting action states are considered identical when there are unitary maps

\[
U_1:\mathcal K_1\to\widetilde{\mathcal K}_1,
\qquad
U_2:\mathcal K_2\to\widetilde{\mathcal K}_2
\]

between their probe-generated subspaces such that

\[
U_2W^{(2)}
=
\widetilde W^{(2)}U_1,
\]

\[
U_1(W^{(2)})^*
=
(\widetilde W^{(2)})^*U_2,
\]

and the unitaries carry all root variables and coordinatewise functions to their counterparts. This appears in [lines 311–338](/tmp/L2_FULL_AUDITED_PROOF.md:311).

So “retain the action of \(W^{(2)}\) in both directions” means:

\[
\boxed{
\text{retain the laws and inner products of every finite computation built
using }W^{(2)},(W^{(2)})^*,\phi,\phi',\text{ and the current variables}.
}
\]

It does not retain irrelevant parts of the operator. The proof explicitly discards the action of \(W^{(2)}\) outside the probe-generated subspaces, because those directions can never influence the future dynamics.

items.text: I’m using the technical-math teaching workflow again because you’re asking to reset the lesson at the theorem’s actual objective. I’ll stay entirely at that level here: what problem the theorem solves, the exact mathematical success criterion, and what it deliberately does not claim.

The theorem’s main goal is not merely to compute the limiting output \(f(t)\). It is to prove that the entire training process of a wide, two-hidden-layer network approaches a well-defined infinite-width dynamical system in which both hidden layers genuinely learn.

## Conceptual goal

For every width \(n\), training is:

- random, because the parameters are randomly initialized;
- discrete, because it uses gradient-descent steps;
- very high-dimensional, with \(n^2\) middle-layer weights;
- width-dependent, because initialization and learning rates change with \(n\).

We ask whether, as \(n\to\infty\), this complicated random system settles into a predictable macroscopic evolution.

There are several ways this could fail:

1. The dynamics might blow up or have no width limit.
2. Only the output weights might learn while the hidden features freeze.
3. The activation might effectively become affine, producing a disguised linear model.
4. A limiting formula might exist but fail to be autonomous: predicting its future might require remembering the entire initialization or training history.
5. Different subsequences of widths might produce different limits.

The theorem rules out all five failures for this particular network and scaling. Its conceptual conclusion is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Wide-network training self-averages into one closed, deterministic,
nonlinear feature-learning flow.}
}
\]

“Deterministic” here means deterministic at the level of laws. The limiting variables can be represented as random variables, but their joint law and its evolution are fixed rather than depending on the particular finite-width initialization.

## Exact mathematical goal

Let \(k\) be the GD iteration and set

\[
t=k\eta_n,\qquad \eta_n=n^{-2}.
\]

Thus observing a fixed macroscopic time \(t\) means running approximately \(tn^2\) GD steps.

The proof uses the exact transformed state

\[
\Theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t)
=
\bigl(X_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t),B_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t),C_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t)\bigr),
\]

where

\[
C_n=nc_n,\qquad
X_n=F(A_n),\qquad
F(a)=a+\frac{a^3}{3}.
\]

Here:

- \(X_n(t)\in\mathbb R^n\) represents the first-layer preactivations through an invertible change of coordinates;
- \(B_n(t)\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is the middle weight matrix;
- \(C_n(t)\in\mathbb R^n\) is the naturally rescaled readout vector.

The primary theorem is the existence of a deterministic continuum state \(\Theta(t)\) such that, for every finite \(T\),

\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
d_{\mathrm{act}}\!\left(
\Theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t),\Theta(t)
\right)
\longrightarrow 0
\quad\text{in probability}.
\]

Explicitly, this means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[
\mathbb P\!\left(
\sup_{0\le t\le T}
d_{\mathrm{act}}\!\left(
\Theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t),\Theta(t)
\right)>\varepsilon
\right)
\longrightarrow0.
\]

The distance \(d_{\mathrm{act}}\) is richer than a distance between ordinary neuron distributions. It tests the joint laws and inner products of every finite collection of quantities generated from the current state using:

- the middle operator \(B\);
- its adjoint \(B^*\);
- the activation and derivative gates;
- finite compositions of those operations.

This richer state is necessary because knowing the law of

\[
S=BH
\]

does not determine the law of

\[
B^*D.
\]

But \(B^*D\) determines the next first-layer velocity. Therefore the marginal laws of the neurons alone do not contain enough information to predict training.

The continuum state evolves autonomously:

\[
\dot X=-2eB^*D,\qquad
\dot B=-2e\,D\otimes H,\qquad
\dot C=-2eG,
\]

with all the derived quantities \(A,H,S,G,D,e\) determined by the current \((X,B,C)\). Autonomy is expressed by the semigroup identity

\[
\Phi_t\bigl(\Phi_s(\Theta_0)\bigr)
=
\Phi_{t+s}(\Theta_0).
\]

So if training is stopped at time \(s\), the action law at that moment contains everything needed to restart it. Neither the original matrix nor the past trajectory must be attached as hidden memory.

The theorem then makes the convergence tangible through the neuron paths. Define the empirical law of the entire first-layer trajectories by

\[
\Lambda_n^A
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\delta_{A_{n,i}(\cdot)}.
\]

This is a probability measure on \(C([0,T])\), the space of continuous real-valued paths. The theorem proves

\[
\Lambda_n^A\longrightarrow \mathcal L(A(\cdot))
\quad\text{in }W_2(C([0,T])),
\]

and similarly

\[
\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{S_{n,j}(\cdot)}
\longrightarrow \mathcal L(S(\cdot)).
\]

Thus it is not merely saying that the neuron distributions converge separately at each time. It says that the distributions of their complete time trajectories converge, including temporal correlations and second moments.

Finally, the theorem must show that the resulting limit is nontrivial. For sufficiently small \(T>0\), it proves

\[
\int_0^T\mathbb E|\dot A(t)|^2\,dt>0,
\qquad
\int_0^T\mathbb E|\dot S(t)|^2\,dt>0.
\]

Therefore both hidden layers really move. It also proves positive displacement:

\[
\mathbb E|A(T)-A(0)|^2>0,\qquad
\mathbb E|S(T)-S(0)|^2>0.
\]

All three parameter blocks contribute positively to training, and the total tangent kernel satisfies

\[
K(t)\neq K(0)
\]

for small nonzero \(t\). This rules out a frozen-kernel limit.

Nonlinearity is expressed by

\[
\inf_{a,b\in\mathbb R}
\mathbb E\left[
\bigl(\arctan Z(t)-a-bZ(t)\bigr)^2
\right]>0
\]

for each hidden preactivation \(Z=A,S\). Hence the activation cannot be replaced, even in mean square under the evolving hidden law, by an affine function.

So the substantive target has three parts:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{Fidelity: exact finite GD converges to the proposed limit;}\\[2mm]
\text{Closure: the current limiting state determines its own future;}\\[2mm]
\text{Nondegeneracy: both hidden layers move and remain genuinely nonlinear.}
\end{array}}
\]

This is a finite-time scaling-limit theorem. It does not claim that the loss eventually reaches zero, that training finds a global optimizer, or that the result already extends to arbitrary datasets and architectures.

items.text: I’m using the named technical-math teaching skill, so I’ll build this as a sequence of self-contained blackboard blocks. This first block will give only the proof architecture—with one stable set of canonical symbols—and then pause before we derive Bridge 1.

Fix a finite time horizon \(T>0\). The proof’s central goal is

\[
\boxed{\text{exact width-}n\text{ GD trajectory}}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\text{unique continuum action-law trajectory}}
\]

uniformly for \(0\le t\le T\), in probability.

We will use these symbols throughout:

- \(\theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t)\): the linearly interpolated exact GD state.
- \(\theta_n(t)\): the corresponding finite-width continuous gradient flow.
- \(\theta_n^\delta(t)\): explicit Euler applied to that flow with a fixed mesh \(\delta>0\).
- \(\Theta^\delta(t)\): Euler applied to the continuum flow with the same mesh.
- \(\Theta(t)\): the exact continuum action-law flow.

All these states use the exact transformed variables

\[
C=nc,\qquad X=F(A),\qquad F(a)=a+\frac{a^3}{3}.
\]

Thus a finite-width state is the triple

\[
\theta_n=(X_n,B_n,C_n),
\]

where \(X_n,C_n\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(B_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). The continuum state is

\[
\Theta=(X,B,C),
\]

where \(X\) and \(C\) are square-integrable random coordinates and \(B\) is a bounded operator between two Hilbert spaces.

The entire convergence proof is the following sandwich:

\[
\theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}
\;\approx\;
\theta_n
\;\approx\;
\theta_n^\delta
\;\longrightarrow\;
\Theta^\delta
\;\approx\;
\Theta.
\]

The order of limits is essential: first \(n\to\infty\) while \(\delta\) is fixed, and only afterward \(\delta\downarrow0\).

### 1. Rewrite the finite network as a dimension-free flow

Direct differentiation of the finite network gives an exact ODE for \((A,B,C)\). The factor \(q(A)=1/(1+A^2)\) appearing in the \(A\)-equation is removed by \(X=F(A)\), because

\[
F'(A)=1+A^2=\frac1{q(A)}.
\]

The resulting equations are exactly

\[
\dot X=-2eB^\top D,\qquad
\dot B=-2e\,D\otimes_n H,\qquad
\dot C=-2eG,
\]

where

\[
A=F^{-1}(X),\quad H=\arctan(A),\quad S=BH,
\]

\[
G=\arctan(S),\quad D=Cq(S),\quad
e=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n C_jG_j-1.
\]

This is an identity at every finite width, not an approximation.

### 2. Prove estimates that do not deteriorate with width

Use the normalized vector norm

\[
\|v\|_n^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2
\]

and the matrix operator norm. The state distance is

\[
\|X-\widetilde X\|_n+
\|B-\widetilde B\|_{\mathrm{op}}+
\|C-\widetilde C\|_n.
\]

On every finite time interval, the proof establishes width-independent bounds on \(B\), \(C\), and the vector field. It then proves a width-independent Lipschitz estimate

\[
\|V_n(\theta)-V_n(\widetilde\theta)\|
\le L_T\|\theta-\widetilde\theta\|,
\]

where \(V_n\) is the preceding ODE vector field and \(L_T\) does not depend on \(n\).

Consequently, finite-width Euler approximation satisfies

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
\|\theta_n^\delta(t)-\theta_n(t)\|
\le C_T\delta,
\]

again with \(C_T\) independent of \(n\). This uniformity is what later permits the mesh to be removed after taking the width limit.

### 3. Construct the continuum flow before taking the limit

The continuum state cannot consist only of the marginal laws of \(A\) and \(S\). The velocity of \(X\) contains \(B^*D\), and the law of \(BH\) does not determine the law of \(B^*D\).

The proof therefore constructs two canonical Hilbert spaces:

\[
\mathcal H_R\quad\text{for first-layer quantities},\qquad
\mathcal H_L\quad\text{for second-layer quantities}.
\]

The initial random matrix becomes a bounded operator

\[
B_0:\mathcal H_R\to\mathcal H_L,
\]

with its genuine Hilbert adjoint \(B_0^*\). On these fixed spaces the continuum equations are

\[
\dot X=-2eB^*D,\qquad
\dot B=-2e\,D\otimes H,\qquad
\dot C=-2eG,
\]

where now

\[
(D\otimes H)v=D\langle H,v\rangle_{\mathcal H_R}.
\]

A contraction argument proves local existence and uniqueness. Energy and norm bounds prevent finite-time blow-up, giving a global solution. Because the future uses only the current \(X,C,B,B^*\) actions, the flow is autonomous and restartable.

### 4. Identify the width limit at a fixed Euler mesh

Fix \(\delta>0\). Then the number of Euler steps before time \(T\),

\[
N=\left\lceil\frac{T}{\delta}\right\rceil,
\]

is finite and independent of \(n\).

The actual Euler scheme is still not directly a fixed tensor program: its scalar coefficients contain empirical inner products that depend on width. The proof therefore introduces an auxiliary population oracle, denoted here by \(\bar\theta_n^\delta\). It replaces those empirical coefficients with the corresponding deterministic inner products from the continuum Euler trajectory.

Because \(\delta\) and \(N\) are fixed, this oracle uses only finitely many applications of \(B_0\) and \(B_0^\top\). The reused-Gaussian tensor-program theorem therefore applies and gives

\[
\bar\theta_n^\delta\longrightarrow\Theta^\delta
\]

for every finite collection of observable probes.

The oracle is not silently identified with the real Euler scheme. Their difference consists of explicit empirical Gram-matrix errors. The tensor theorem makes those errors tend to zero, and a discrete Gronwall estimate gives

\[
\sup_{k\le N}
\|\theta_{n,k}^\delta-\bar\theta_{n,k}^\delta\|
\longrightarrow0.
\]

Therefore, at every fixed mesh,

\[
\theta_n^\delta\longrightarrow\Theta^\delta.
\]

This is the only point where the research-level tensor-program theorem enters.

### 5. Remove the mesh

The triangle inequality gives, schematically,

\[
\|\theta_n-\Theta\|
\le
\underbrace{\|\theta_n-\theta_n^\delta\|}_{\le C_T\delta}
+
\underbrace{\|\theta_n^\delta-\Theta^\delta\|}_{\to0\text{ as }n\to\infty}
+
\underbrace{\|\Theta^\delta-\Theta\|}_{\le C_T\delta}.
\]

First fix \(\delta\) and let \(n\to\infty\). The middle term disappears. Then let \(\delta\downarrow0\). The two outer terms disappear.

This proves convergence of the finite-width continuous flow:

\[
\theta_n\longrightarrow\Theta.
\]

The convergence topology records every finite collection of quantities produced by nested applications of \(B\), \(B^*\), and the coordinatewise nonlinearities. This is precisely enough information to determine the action law.

### 6. Return from continuous flow to exact discrete GD

The \(B\)- and \(C\)-updates of exact GD are already Euler updates for the transformed ODE. Only the \(X=F(A)\) update has an extra defect.

Because \(F\) is cubic, that defect can be calculated exactly rather than bounded by an unspecified Taylor remainder. Accumulating it over the interval gives

\[
\sup_{t\le T}
\|\theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}(t)-\theta_n(t)\|
\le
C_T\bigl(
\eta_n+\eta_n\sqrt n+\eta_n^2n
\bigr).
\]

With \(\eta_n=n^{-2}\), the right-hand side is

\[
C_T\left(n^{-2}+n^{-3/2}+n^{-3}\right)\longrightarrow0.
\]

Combining this with the previous bridge proves

\[
\theta_n^{\mathrm{GD}}\longrightarrow\Theta.
\]

Path-law convergence, kernel convergence, and positive feature motion are not automatic consequences of this state convergence. They require three final upgrades: time-equicontinuity for whole paths, truncation and uniform tail control for the unbounded backpropagated field, and the explicit small-time expansion that proves both hidden layers actually move. Those form the final proof block after the convergence mechanism above.
